title: Bihar Brick Kiln Children Get Classrooms at Work Through Neev Ki Eent Foundation
excerpt: Anshu Kumar Jaiswal's foundation pairs on-site Akshar Learning Centres in Sheikhpura with help obtaining Aadhaar, ration and health cards for migrant kiln families.
body:
• Anshu Kumar Jaiswal founded the Neev Ki Eent Foundation in 2023 to keep children of Bihar's brick kiln workers in learning when their families migrate for work.
  • Its Akshar Learning Centres teach foundational reading, writing and mathematics at the kilns themselves, then prepare children to enter or rejoin formal schools.
  • Under Project Swabhimaan in Sheikhpura, about 55 brick kilns are in scope, and more than 15,000 documentation needs — birth certificates, Aadhaar, ration and Ayushman cards — have been identified or addressed, according to the foundation.
  • For diaspora readers who support education causes in Bihar, the foundation's model pairs schooling with the documents families need to claim rations, healthcare and welfare schemes wherever they move.

When a family in Bihar leaves its village for months of work at a brick kiln, the children usually go with it. School is often far away, documents are missing, and learning stops. Anshu Kumar Jaiswal first saw that pattern at close quarters in Sheikhpura between 2019 and 2021, while working as a Gandhi Fellow with the Piramal Foundation, according to YourStory. In 2023 he established the Neev Ki Eent Foundation to address it.

The foundation works with migrant families employed at brick kilns. Its premise is direct: if a child must stay where the family works, education should be made accessible there, rather than waiting for the family to return home.

"For us, education does not simply mean that a child's name is entered into a school register. The real question is whether the child continues to learn."

— Anshu Kumar Jaiswal, founder, Neev Ki Eent Foundation

Taking education where the children are

The foundation's main vehicle is Project Swabhimaan, led in Sheikhpura by Collector and District Magistrate Shekhar Anand and launched district-wide in February 2026, YourStory reported. Its learning arm, the Akshar Learning Centres, provides foundational instruction in reading, writing and mathematics at or near kiln sites, with the stated aim of preparing children to transition into the formal education system.

The Better India, in earlier reporting on the same centres in Sasaram, described local youth — Swabhimaan Fellows recruited from kiln communities — teaching children who had previously spent days moulding clay and carrying bricks. It reported more than 400 children enrolled in the centres in one year and impact touching over 3,000 children.

Documents as the other half of schooling

The foundation treats identity paperwork as part of education, not a separate problem. Families at kilns often lack birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, bank accounts and Ayushman health cards. Without them, access to schooling, rations, healthcare and social security is blocked.

According to Anshu, more than 15,000 documentation-related needs have been identified or addressed across those categories, and around 55 brick kilns in Sheikhpura have been brought within the initiative's scope, with efforts under way to reach thousands of migrant workers and children. The work also includes heat-resilient spaces for families who labour for long hours in intense heat, combining cooling, childcare, education and community activities.

Local youth, not outside help alone

A Swabhimaan Fellowship trains young people from the communities themselves to support children's education, inform families about government schemes and act as a bridge to the administration. The foundation also works alongside government institutions rather than building a parallel system.

"Our objective is not to create a parallel system separate from the government. Our role is to reduce the distance between communities and the system."

— Anshu Kumar Jaiswal

Anshu studied mass communication and later earned a master's degree in social work specialising in youth and community development. He previously worked with the Aspirational Districts Programme, Parliament, the Ministry of Labour and Employment and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, and represented India at the ASEAN-India Youth Summit and a youth exchange programme in China, according to YourStory.

What comes next

The foundation is now working on a model that can be replicated in other brick kiln communities across Bihar. Seasonal migration has shaped Bihar's rural economy for decades, so the test of the Sheikhpura approach is whether learning and documents can travel with a family — whether a child can keep studying despite a move, and whether a family can retain access to services wherever work takes it.
